extracted.intended_audience: researchers, referees, and journals involved in ML-based scientific research (authors of ML-based science papers and reviewers enforcing reporting standards)
extracted.subtask_description: A consensus checklist (REFORMS) for designing, conducting, and reporting ML-based scientific studies to improve validity, reproducibility, and generalizability. It is intended for authors preparing ML-supported scientific claims, referees reviewing such work, and journals setting reporting requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: 1a. Population or distribution about which the scientific claim is made
rubrics_metrics.description: The population of interest is the group to which the researchers intend the findings of the study to generalize — analogous to a “distribution” of scientific interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define the population/distribution clearly (population and distribution treated interchangeably). Explain boundaries of conclusions and how the population shapes uncertainty and significance metrics. Distinguish population from sampling frame and sample. Many papers fail to state this clearly; explicit definition is required so readers can judge generality of ML-based claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: 1b. Motivation for choosing this population or distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the motivation for choosing the population or distribution about which the claim is made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why the chosen population is of interest (scientific reasons or applied need). State whether choice arose deductively (theory-driven), inductively (data-driven), or iteratively, and justify the approach. If motivated by available data, acknowledge this and clarify implications for inference and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 1c. Motivation for the use of ML methods in the study
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the motivation for the use of ML methods in the study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why ML is appropriate relative to traditional statistical methods — e.g., for predictive accuracy, handling large or unstructured data, or answering specific scientific questions. Clarify how the ML task maps to the scientific claim (how model performance supports the claim). Note differences between ML methods research, predictive analytics, explanatory modeling, and simulation, and justify inclusion of ML accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2a. Dataset description and unique identifier
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the dataset used for training and evaluating the model and provide a link or DOI to uniquely identify the dataset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report dataset provenance, versions, and unique identifiers (links/DOIs). Distinguish training and evaluation datasets if applicable. Provide sufficient documentation so others can locate the exact data used; note time of collection and any access conditions. If not shareable, explain restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2b. Code details and unique identifier
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide details about the code used to train and evaluate the model and produce the results reported in the paper along with link or DOI to uniquely identify the version of the code used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Share code with a persistent link/DOI and versioning (e.g., commit hash). Include exact scripts used for training, evaluation, preprocessing, and result generation. If proprietary components exist, document them and explain their role and limitations for reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2c. Computing infrastructure description
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the computing infrastructure used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report hardware and software environment details (CPU/GPU types, memory, OS, library versions). Note nondeterministic behaviors or external dependencies (e.g., cloud services, proprietary models) that affect reproducibility. This helps others understand feasibility and potential differences when reproducing results.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2d. README with reproduction instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a README file which contains instructions for generating the results using the provided dataset and code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include clear, step-by-step instructions, dependencies, configuration settings, and expected outputs. Make it easy for an independent researcher to run the code and understand the workflow. Prefer simple reproducibility routes such as scripts or containerized environments.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2e. Reproduction script for all reported results
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a reproduction script to produce all results reported in the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supply runnable scripts that generate the main tables, figures, and metrics from the provided data and code. This lowers the barrier to verifying claims and detecting errors; where full automation is impossible, document manual steps explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: 3a. Data sources, collection time, and ground-truth annotation process
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe source(s) of data, separately for the training and evaluation datasets (if applicable), along with the time when the dataset(s) are collected, the source and process of ground-truth annotations, and other data documentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report provenance for each dataset partition, dates of collection, how labels/ground truth were produced (annotators, protocols, interrater reliability), and available metadata. Provide data documentation (schemas, dictionaries) to aid interpretation and reuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: 3b. Sampling frame (distribution or set from which dataset is sampled)
rubrics_metrics.description: State the distribution or set from which the dataset is sampled (i.e., the sampling frame).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify the sampling frame and how the sample was drawn from it. Describe inclusion/exclusion criteria and selection mechanisms. This connects the dataset to the stated population/distribution (Item 1a) and informs generalizability judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: 3c. Justify dataset usefulness for the modeling task
rubrics_metrics.description: Justify why the dataset is useful for the modeling task at hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain relevance of features, outcome prevalence, size, and representativeness for the research question. Discuss suitability for the specific ML task and potential biases introduced by dataset limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: 3d. Outcome variable definition and descriptive statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: State the outcome variable of the model, along with descriptive statistics (split by class for a categorical outcome variable) and its definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define precisely the target variable, how it was constructed, and any transformations. Provide class counts, prevalence, and summary statistics that help interpret model performance and potential class imbalance issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: 3e. Sample size and outcome frequencies
rubrics_metrics.description: State the sample size and outcome frequencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report total N and counts per relevant partition (train/validation/test; classes; subgroups). This informs power, stability of estimates, and uncertainty quantification.

rubrics_metrics.name: 3f. Missing data rates
rubrics_metrics.description: State the percentage of missing data, split by class for a categorical outcome variable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report missingness patterns and rates overall and by class or subgroup. Describe whether missingness is item-level or sample-level and provide diagnostics or rationale about missingness mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: 3g. Justify representativeness of dataset relative to population
rubrics_metrics.description: Justify why the distribution or set from which the dataset is drawn (3b) is representative of the one about which the scientific claim is being made (1a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide evidence or reasoning for representativeness (coverage, sampling biases, demographic comparisons). Discuss limitations and potential effects on external validity; when representativeness is weak, explicitly state implications for the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4a. Describe sample exclusions with rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe whether any samples are excluded with a rationale for why they are excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report exclusion criteria and counts removed at each step (e.g., CONSORT-like flowchart). Explain rationales (e.g., corrupted data, out-of-scope instances) and check sensitivity to exclusion choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4b. Handling of impossible or corrupt samples
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe how impossible or corrupt samples are dealt with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document detection and remediation procedures for corrupted, impossible, or invalid records. Explain imputation, removal, or correction strategies and their justification. Where possible, quantify impact of these choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4c. Describe all transformations from raw data to model input
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe all transformations of the dataset from its raw form (3a) to the form used in the model, for instance, treatment of missing data and normalization—preferably through a flow chart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a clear pipeline of preprocessing steps (tokenization, feature engineering, normalization, encoding, aggregation). Prefer visual flow charts and explicit ordering to reveal potential leakage and to allow reproduction; include software versions and parameters used.

rubrics_metrics.name: 5a. Describe all models trained in detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe, in detail, all models trained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List model classes, architectures, training objectives, initialization, and implementation details. Include any ensembling, transfer learning, or pretrained components used. Being explicit enables understanding of model behaviors and reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: 5b. Justify choice of model types implemented
rubrics_metrics.description: Justify the choice of model types implemented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why particular model families were selected given the task, data, and scientific question. Discuss trade-offs (interpretability vs performance), and whether choices were theory-driven or exploratory.

rubrics_metrics.name: 5c. Describe evaluation method including data splits
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the method for evaluating the model(s) reported in the paper, including details of train-test splits or cross-validation folds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report exact splitting strategies (holdout, k-fold, nested CV), random seeds, stratification criteria, and any grouping constraints (e.g., patient-level splits). Justify chosen evaluation strategy given temporal/spatial/dependent data structure; discuss dependence-aware CV when applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: 5d. Describe the method for selecting reported model(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the method for selecting the model(s) reported in the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain selection criteria (validation metric, early stopping, hyperparameter selection process). Clarify whether reported model is best on validation, test, or chosen for interpretability; avoid selection on test set and describe any model selection pipelines used.

rubrics_metrics.name: 5e. Specify hyperparameter tuning details for reported models
rubrics_metrics.description: For the model(s) reported in the paper, specify details about the hyperparameter tuning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report search space, search method (grid, random, Bayesian), number of trials, tuning metric, and whether tuning used nested CV. Include ranges, discrete choices, and default values, and document computational budget or constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: 5f. Justify that comparisons are against appropriate baselines
rubrics_metrics.description: Justify that model comparisons are against appropriate baselines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare to simple and strong baselines (including domain-specific heuristics and naive predictors). Explain why chosen baselines are appropriate and include well-tuned baselines to avoid misleading claims from weak comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: 6a. Justify absence of leakage from test data into preprocessing/modeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Justify that preprocessing (Module 4) and modeling (Module 5) steps only use information from the training dataset (and not the test dataset).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how preprocessing and feature engineering were applied within training folds (e.g., fit scalers only on training data). Provide evidence or documentation that test data were held out and not used for tuning or normalization to avoid optimistic bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: 6b. Describe methods to address dependencies/duplicates between train and test
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe methods used to address dependencies or duplicates between the training and test datasets (e.g. different samples from the same patients are kept in the same dataset partition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document grouping strategies (by patient, household, time window) or deduplication procedures. Explain handling of nonindependent observations and provide checks for leakage due to duplicated or related samples across partitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 6c. Justify legitimacy of features to avoid leakage
rubrics_metrics.description: Justify that each feature or input used in the model is legitimate for the task at hand and does not lead to leakage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether features are causally prior to the prediction target and available at prediction time. Identify proxy variables that inadvertently encode target information or future data and either remove or explicitly justify their inclusion; document feature provenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: 7a. State metrics and justify metric used for model selection
rubrics_metrics.description: State all metrics used to assess and compare model performance (e.g., accuracy, AUROC etc.). Justify that the metric used to select the final model is suitable for the task.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report primary and secondary metrics, per-class metrics where appropriate, calibration, and decision-threshold-dependent measures. Justify metric relevance to the scientific question and real-world costs; avoid relying on a single misleading metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: 7b. State uncertainty estimates and calculation details
rubrics_metrics.description: State uncertainty estimates (e.g., confidence intervals, standard deviations), and give details of how these are calculated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide uncertainty quantification for performance estimates (bootstrap, CV-based, analytic intervals). Describe methods, assumptions, seeds, and how intervals are computed; report variability across runs and sensitivity to modeling choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: 7c. Justify statistical tests and check assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Justify the choice of statistical tests (if used) and a check for the assumptions of the statistical test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain test selection (paired/unpaired, parametric/nonparametric), correction for multiple comparisons, and assumptions (independence, distributional). Provide diagnostics or alternative approaches when assumptions are violated.

rubrics_metrics.name: 8a. Describe evidence of external validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe evidence of external validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report external validation experiments, replication on distinct datasets, or domain generalization analyses. Discuss empirical evidence showing whether findings hold beyond the original sampling frame and what limits apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: 8b. Describe contexts where findings do not hold
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe contexts in which the authors do not expect the study’s findings to hold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State limitations, likely failure modes, ethical or demographic contexts where models may underperform, and any assumptions that restrict generalizability. Explicitly discuss scenarios that could invalidate claims and recommend caution or future validation.
